extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, induction, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and guidance for discovering laws of causation by observation and experiment, including how causes combine, when effects are deducible, and what good observation requires. Emphasizes distinctions between mechanical (compositional) and chemical/biological (non-compositional) cases and the role of mental analysis preceding experimental separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint effect of several causes is identical with the sum of their separate effects; in such cases the same law which expresses the effect of each cause acting by itself also correctly expresses the part due to that cause when acting with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplified in mechanics (composition of forces): if two forces act simultaneously they produce the combined displacement equal to the separate displacements added. Where composition holds, deductive prediction of combined effects from separate laws is possible. Use this principle when causes do not alter one another's modes of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compositional (heteropathic) combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases in which the conjunction of causes produces effects heterogeneous to those of the causes individually; new laws arise on combination so that the compound exhibits properties not traceable to the separate elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical examples: hydrogen + oxygen → water (properties not sum of constituents); taste of sugar of lead not sum of acetic acid and lead; biological/physiological phenomena likewise produce new laws (life). In such cases induction cannot deduce outcomes from separate-element laws alone — specific experiment is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of mutual interference of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between (a) cases where concurrent causes 'add' (including algebraic subtraction when opposing) so that each exerts full effect (e.g., stream into reservoir vs drain), and (b) cases where combination gives rise to entirely new phenomena (e.g., two liquids forming a solid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether apparent cancellation still reflects the sum of separate effects (difference-as-sum) or whether the union invokes new 'heteropathic' laws. The former can be analyzed by algebraic reasoning; the latter requires experimental discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional validity of proportionality of effects to causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom that effects are proportional to their causes is a special case of composition and holds when causes are homogeneous and do not change the kind of effect produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportionality fails where augmentation of cause changes the kind of effect (e.g., heat: small quantity increases bulk, double melts, triple decomposes). Apply proportional reasoning only within the range where the principle of composition holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of some laws across combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some properties and laws (e.g., weight additivity) remain rigidly fulfilled in every combination into which objects enter; component parts retain mechanical and chemical properties unless superseded by new laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which attributes/laws are invariant under combination (candidates for deductive use) and which may be superseded by emergent laws. Use invariant properties as reliable premises when composing effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composability of heteropathic laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws produced by non-compositional combinations (heteropathic laws) may themselves be capable of composition with one another and with original physical/chemical laws; complex phenomena may be deducible from simpler 'laws of life' or intermediate combination-laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests a route toward making chemistry and physiology more deductive: search for intermediate-level laws (e.g., law of definite proportions, Berthollet's law, isomorphism) from which properties of compounds may be inferred without direct experiment on every new combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main aim of Induction: ascertain laws of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction's principal business is to determine what causes are correctly assigned to what effects, and what effects follow from what causes; knowing these would amount to being acquainted with the whole course of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame inductive inquiries explicitly as assignments of causes to effects. Use discovered causal laws to explain uniformities and to predict individual events given sufficient antecedent data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation as analytical decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining causal connexions is in effect an analysis: decompose complex antecedents and consequents into component parts; the mental partition of phenomena is an indispensable first step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation is not mere seeing but seeing parts and relations. Begin with a careful mental analysis before attempting experimental separation. Be aware that different observers vary greatly in their power to decompose complex phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of experiment to separate facts in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine on which antecedents each consequent is invariably attendant, one must effect a separation of facts not only mentally but in nature — i.e., by experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that isolate candidate antecedents while holding collateral conditions constant to reveal true causal links. Mental analysis suggests which separations to attempt; experiment tests them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good observer
rubrics_metrics.description: A good observer discerns component parts, avoids confusing observation with imagination or inference, records kinds and degrees accurately, and divides phenomena into appropriate parts rather than making awkward or careless partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid common anti-patterns: inattention (overlooking facts), conflating observation with inference or imagination, vague assessment of degrees/quantities, and improper partitioning (either over-separating or lumping distinct parts). Training and self-education improve observational skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rules of observation and art of observing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not properly an 'Art of Observing' that teaches the mechanical doing; rather, there may be rules of observing which are instructions for preparing and educating the mind to be capable of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat observational rules as self-education directives (preparing one's intellect), not as step-by-step mechanical procedures. Focus on cultivating mental habits that make accurate observation more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterministic grounding: every fact has a cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Every fact which begins to exist has a cause, and the present facts are the result of past facts; thus the order of nature presents a complex uniformity resolvable into simpler uniformities (antecedents to consequents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this presupposition to motivate analytic and experimental inquiry: seek the antecedent portions responsible for particular consequents. Recognize the practical impossibility of reconstructing the entire universe's prior state, hence the need to focus on relevant antecedents.
